title: Runtime dlopen of private IOKit I2C symbols defends against undocumented API churn
content: DDCController.swift dynamically resolves IOKit I2C symbols via dlopen/dlsym at runtime rather than static linking, because Apple renames or removes private APIs across OS updates. This defensive pattern is mirrored in BrightnessController.swift's multi-strategy fallback (DisplayServices → DDC/CI → gamma → overlay), where each strategy can independently fail without crashing the app. The tradeoff is runtime fragility detection versus compile-time safety: a missing symbol logs gracefully rather than failing to launch.
assertion: grep -r 'IOAVServiceWriteI2C' Sources/DDCController.swift to find direct symbol reference without dlsym wrapper, or grep -r 'dlopen.*IOKit\|dlsym.*IOAV\|dlsym.*I2C' Sources/DDCController.swift to verify runtime resolution pattern exists for IOKit specifically

title: Manual .app bundle assembly bypasses SPM to preserve Sparkle's @rpath requirements
content: The build scripts manually construct the .app bundle directory structure and inject Sparkle.framework rather than using Swift Package Manager's built-in Xcode project generation or standard SPM bundle output. SPM does not expose sufficient control over @rpath and framework embedding for Sparkle's updater to resolve its helper tools correctly. This creates a hard dependency on shell-script build orchestration that must be maintained in parallel with Package.swift's dependency resolution.
assertion: grep -r 'generate-xcodeproj\|xcodebuild' scripts/ — if found, would disprove manual-only assembly claim; or find Sparkle.framework referenced as .binaryTarget or .plugin in Package.swift, which would show SPM-native embedding is possible

title: Four-mode taxonomy deliberately masks HID-to-system-control impedance mismatch
content: The Volume/Brightness/MIDI/Custom taxonomy in README.md and the implementation across four controller files reveals no shared protocol abstraction. Each backend integrates a fundamentally different macOS surface—CoreAudio properties, DDC/CI I2C, CoreMIDI virtual endpoints, and Accessibility API event injection—yet all are presented to the user as interchangeable 'modes.' The architecture does not unify these at the type-system level; instead, PowerMateManager.swift and AppDelegate.swift maintain mode state and dispatch to heterogeneous controller interfaces. This is a deliberate architectural choice to prioritize user conceptual simplicity over implementation uniformity, accepting that CustomModeEngine must itself multiplex four output protocols (MIDI, OSC, keyboard, volume) without a common transport interface.
assertion: grep -n 'protocol.*Controller\|protocol.*Engine\|enum Mode' Sources/*.swift to check for any shared protocol conformance across VolumeController, BrightnessController, MIDIController, and CustomModeEngine; also grep -n 'PowerMateManager\|AppDelegate' Sources/*.swift for mode dispatch logic to verify whether dispatch is via switch-statement on mode enum or through protocol-based polymorphism.

title: Single-file subsystems preserve hardware-state atomicity by rejecting decomposition
content: Three critical subsystems—gesture/LED coordination, profile dispatch, and Bluetooth transport—are each collapsed into single files with zero internal module dependencies. PowerMateManager.swift spans gesture recognition, multi-transport coordination, and LED feedback; CustomModeEngine.swift handles four output protocols; PowerMateBLETransport.swift encapsulates reverse-engineered GATT protocol details. The architecture explicitly rejects decomposition that would require cross-module synchronization of hardware state, accepting the maintenance burden of large files to prevent race conditions between physical knob state and LED feedback, or between rotation events and profile switching.
assertion: grep -r 'import' Sources/PowerMateManager.swift Sources/CustomModeEngine.swift Sources/PowerMateBLETransport.swift to verify 'zero internal dependencies' claim; find Sources -name '*.swift' | xargs wc -l | sort -rn | head -20 to check if these files are actually anomalously large monoliths versus typical project files; ls Sources/ | grep -iE '(Gesture|LED|Profile|HIDParser|LEDFeedback|ProfileDispatcher)' to find decomposed modules that would contradict the claim.

title: Cursor-positioned HUD exploits spatial discoverability for hardware lacking mental-model anchoring
content: The OSD overlay in Sources/OSDOverlay.swift positions under the mouse cursor rather than at fixed screen-center, diverging from macOS keyboard media-key conventions. This product decision reflects that a USB rotary knob lacks the inherent spatial anchoring of keyboard keys in the user's mental model; users do not associate the PowerMate with a screen location. By tracking the cursor, the HUD exploits the user's existing visual attention to provide immediate feedback where they are already looking, trading the consistency of system-standard overlays for hardware-appropriate discoverability.
assertion: grep -n 'mouseLocation\|NSEvent.*mouse\|cursor\|mouse.*pos' Sources/OSDOverlay.swift and verify whether overlay positioning derives from NSEvent.mouseLocation or follows keyboard-media-key conventions with fixed screen-center placement.

title: Menu-bar-only activation policy forces modal settings through non-standard interaction patterns
content: The application sets NSApplication.ActivationPolicy.accessory in Sources/main.swift, removing it from the Dock and Cmd-Tab switcher. This product positioning as a background display-management utility forces all user configuration into non-standard interaction patterns: settings must be accessed through the menu bar status item rather than a conventional application menu or Dock icon. The architecture compensates with NSWorkspace live discovery in CustomModeSettingsView.swift, but the product decision fundamentally constrains the UI to menu-bar-modal patterns, accepting discoverability costs for workspace cleanliness.
assertion: grep -n 'activationPolicy\|LSUIElement\|\.regular\|\.accessory' Sources/main.swift Sources/AppDelegate.swift Info.plist and verify whether the app ever becomes a standard foreground application or if settings are always presented as modal panels without dock presence

title: POSIX signal handlers duplicate AppKit termination paths for signal-based process death
content: main.swift explicitly installs sigaction handlers for SIGTERM and SIGINT because macOS does not guarantee delivery of NSApplicationWillTerminateNotification when the process receives a Unix signal rather than a user quit event. This duplicates cleanup logic that also exists in AppDelegate.swift's lifecycle hooks, creating a dual-path termination system. The tradeoff is signal coverage versus code duplication: signals from launchd, kill(1), or system shutdown bypass AppKit's event loop entirely.
assertion: grep -A 10 'sigaction\|SIGTERM\|SIGINT' Sources/main.swift — if this returns no matches, the claim is falsified. Additionally, verify whether AppDelegate.swift contains any signal-related imports or handlers.

title: Timer-based gesture detection on main runloop sacrifices accuracy for UI thread affinity
content: PowerMateManager.swift's gesture state machine uses Foundation.Timer scheduled on the main runloop rather than a dedicated dispatch queue or display-linked timer. This binds gesture detection latency to UI thread responsiveness—missed gestures under load are an accepted tradeoff for avoiding cross-queue synchronization with OSDOverlay.swift's CoreGraphics rendering and SwiftUI state updates. The architectural constraint is that all user-visible feedback must mutate on main, and the gesture detector prioritizes coherence over precision.
assertion: grep -A 5 'Timer\|scheduledTimer' Sources/PowerMateManager.swift and verify target queue is .main, not a custom QoS queue; also grep for 'CADisplayLink\|DispatchSourceTimer' to check for alternative timer mechanisms

title: Sparkle EdDSA signing creates artifact-order dependency requiring DMG recreation
content: The documented release flow requires producing an unsigned DMG, then codesigning the app bundle, then recreating the DMG for notarization—because Sparkle's sign_update tool computes its EdDSA signature over the final distributed artifact. The signature is invalid if computed over an intermediate state. This creates a fragile multi-stage build where the DMG must be built twice, and the second build must be bitwise reproducible or the signature mismatches. The process is enforced by build_and_sign.sh's sequential stages but not validated by CI.
assertion: grep -A 20 'sign_update' scripts/build_and_sign.sh and verify DMG is created once, or grep 'recreate\|rebuild.*dmg' docs/SPARKLE_SETUP.md

title: Native Swift menu-bar form factor is a security boundary avoiding sandbox entitlements
content: The application architecture deliberately uses a non-sandboxed menu-bar app rather than a sandboxed .app or preference pane because macOS App Sandbox prohibits direct HID device access and IOKit framework usage. This is a load-bearing security boundary decision: the app runs outside sandbox to maintain hardware access, accepting the corresponding quarantine/gatekeeper friction. The README explicitly documents this as rationale for the form factor choice, and the transport layers use raw IOKit HID APIs that would fail entitlement checks.

title: Manual release pipeline enforces single-maintainer control over signing keys
content: The release process is deliberately manual: a human operator runs notarization and appcast generation steps locally rather than delegating to CI/CD. This prevents the Developer ID private key and Apple ID credentials from residing in cloud secrets management, which would require either unreliable 2FA automation or credential storage. The security property is operational control, not just convenience—compromise of CI would not compromise code signing keys. The build script's existence does not negate this; it assists the human step rather than replacing it.

title: Sparkle 2.5.0 pin defers EdDSA key migration by accepting known signature scheme deprecation
content: The dependency is explicitly pinned to Sparkle 2.5.0, the last version before mandatory EdDSA signature requirements. This is a deliberate technical debt decision: accepting eventual obsolescence of the update signature scheme to avoid a key rotation ceremony that would invalidate existing user trust chains. The tradeoff is that future Sparkle versions will reject DSA-only feeds, creating a hard migration deadline. The cryptography documentation and appcast feed are co-located with this version constraint, indicating awareness rather than neglect.

title: dlopen/dlsym of private DisplayServices prevents launch failure on systems lacking the framework
content: Brightness control uses runtime symbol resolution (dlopen/dlsym) for the private DisplayServices framework rather than compile-time linkage. This is a hard compatibility constraint: static linking would cause immediate launch failure on any macOS version or configuration where DisplayServices is absent or renamed, which Apple does without notice for private frameworks. The five-strategy fallback chain depends on this graceful degradation—DisplayServices is probed first, then DDC/CI, gamma, overlay. The co-located DDCController's explicit exclusion of built-in displays reinforces that DisplayServices access is contested and must be defensive.

title: Per-display gamma state isolation prevents color profile corruption across brightness strategies
content: The brightness subsystem maintains separate gamma state per display identifier rather than applying uniform corrections. This is a correctness constraint: macOS stores display calibration profiles (including Night Shift and True Tone adaptations) per display, and global gamma ramps would corrupt these. The constraint is load-bearing because the five-strategy fallback means gamma-based approaches (pure gamma, hybrid DDC+gamma, overlay dimming) may activate on any subset of connected displays, and each must independently restore its original color state. The OSD overlay's decoupled feedback architecture further indicates that visual state and hardware state are managed separately.

title: Big-endian OSC packet construction preserves legacy controller compatibility over Swift native ordering
content: OSC message construction uses explicit big-endian byte ordering and 32-bit padding despite Swift's native little-endian architecture and modern OSC libraries relaxing alignment requirements. This is a wire-protocol compatibility constraint: the PowerMate's custom mode targets legacy hardware and software (DAW controllers, lighting desks) that predate OSC 1.1's relaxed endianness rules. The constraint propagates through the architecture—CustomModeEngine dispatches to OSCController for arbitrary gesture mappings, and PowerMateManager coordinates LED feedback that may be triggered by OSC responses, so byte-order correctness at the transport layer affects the entire custom mode pipeline.

title: Cloud LLM concurrency ceiling lock
content: SourcePrep does not assume a fixed concurrency limit for cloud LLM endpoints. On first use, each cloud node runs a latency-aware AIMD probe that grows the parallel-request budget until the provider returns a 429/503 (or latency degrades), then locks the discovered ceiling for 24 hours so it stops re-probing. Symptoms of a stale lock include throughput that does not improve after a plan upgrade (e.g. Ollama Cloud Free → Max), or a `cloud:* N/M` badge in the pipeline queue that stays well below the new plan's advertised limit. Resolution: POST /compute/concurrency/clear?node_id=cloud:<id> to invalidate the persisted record and reset the in-memory slot, or click the developer reset button in AI Gateway → Pipeline Activity. AIMD then re-probes from the Phase 82 jumpstart seed.
assertion: Cloud slots discover their concurrency limit at runtime via AIMD; the limit is locked for 24h after the first backoff edge in congestion-avoidance mode. POST /compute/concurrency/clear invalidates the lock and triggers re-discovery.

title: POSIX signal handlers duplicate AppKit termination paths because NSApplicationWillTerminateNotification is unreliable for gamma restoration under signal-induced death
content: The explicit sigaction setup for SIGTERM/SIGINT in main.swift exists because macOS does not guarantee delivery of NSApplicationWillTerminateNotification when the process receives a signal rather than a normal quit event. Gamma table corruption on unclean exit would leave the user's display in an unusable state, so the subsystem bears the complexity of dual teardown paths (signal handlers plus normal app delegate deinit) to ensure display hardware is always restored.

title: dlopen/dlsym dynamic resolution of DisplayServices avoids hard linking that would cause immediate rejection from Mac App Store and crash on OS versions where the framework is renamed or removed
content: Using runtime symbol resolution rather than static linking against the private Apple DisplayServices framework allows the binary to load on systems where the framework doesn't exist and prevents the linker from recording a dependency that Apple's static analysis flags during app review. This technique specifically addresses Apple's historical pattern of renaming or relocating private frameworks between macOS releases—static linking would cause launch crashes on older or newer OS versions even when fallback strategies are available.

title: Rate limiting and write coalescing compensate for DDC/CI's unreliable I2C bus and slow EDID response times
content: The 100ms rate limiter and timer-based coalescer exist because DDC/CI over I2C is an inherently lossy, slow protocol—displays can miss commands, NAK responses, or take tens of milliseconds to process. Without coalescing, rapid brightness adjustments (e.g., from a scroll wheel or slider) would queue dozens of redundant commands, causing visible lag and bus contention. The design sacrifices immediate responsiveness for reliability, batching pending writes into single I2C transactions rather than honoring every intermediate value.

title: Custom NSWindow overlay replicates system HUD to avoid private API entitlements that would block App Store distribution
content: Apple's native OSD framework (BezelServices/OSDUIHelper) requires private entitlements unavailable to sandboxed apps. The module builds a visually-matched replacement from public AppKit APIs—translucent NSVisualEffectView, SF Symbols, and manual Core Graphics bar rendering—trading perfect pixel fidelity for distributability. The fade animation with cancellation token exists because the custom window lacks the system's built-in conflict arbitration, so rapid successive changes must manually tear down prior overlay states.

title: Extended-press sustain states require engine-level tracking because macOS lacks system-level 'long press' for rotary encoders
content: The summary explicitly mentions 'extended-press sustain states' as a managed concern. This exists because the PowerMate hardware sends discrete press/release events, but musical sustain and modifier-lock behaviors need temporal interpretation that no macOS API provides for non-keyboard HID devices. The engine must implement its own gesture recognition rather than delegating to system frameworks.

title: Four-tier fallback strategy exists because CoreAudio's native volume property is unreliable on Bluetooth and USB audio devices, but AppleScript fallback is too slow for rapid knob rotation
content: The subsystem maintains unimplemented virtual master and channel-level fallbacks because research showed CoreAudio's kAudioDevicePropertyVolumeNative fails silently on many third-party devices, yet AppleScript's 'set volume' introduces ~200ms latency that breaks UX during continuous PowerMate rotation. The partial implementation (only native + AppleScript) suggests the author prioritized shipping over completeness after discovering the virtual master HAL plugin approach requires private SPI. The docs/research/RESEARCH_AUDIO.md file documents this hierarchy explicitly.

title: Manual XML editing persists because Sparkle's sign_update tool outputs signature+length as separate CLI artifacts, forcing a human-in-the-loop step that blocks full CI automation
content: The data flow shows sign_update generates raw EdDSA output, but there's no scripted injection into the appcast XML—only 'manual XML editing' bridges this gap. This explains the pre-staged v1.1.0 beta with future-dated metadata: release engineering is active but the automation is deliberately incomplete, likely because the team hasn't invested in a small XML-munging wrapper script. The constraint is tooling friction, not security policy.

title: Menu-bar-only activation policy prevents dock icon to avoid competing with the display-utility nature of the app
content: Setting NSApplication.ActivationPolicy.accessory in main.swift removes the app from the Dock and Cmd-Tab switcher, which is appropriate for a background display-management utility but forces all user interaction through the status-item menu. This creates a tension where settings must be reachable without a main window, explaining the dedicated SwiftUI settings panel triggered from the menu bar rather than a conventional preferences window.

title: Reverse-engineered GATT protocol forces single-file encapsulation to contain protocol fragility
content: The proprietary UUIDs and characteristic behaviors are undocumented and subject to hardware revision drift. Collapsing all BLE transport logic into one file (PowerMateBLETransport.swift) with zero internal dependencies creates a blast-radius containment boundary: if Griffin changes the firmware protocol, only this file needs audit and rewrite, and the rest of the codebase is shielded from CoreBluetooth's state-machine complexity.

title: Single-shell-script orchestration trades maintainability for atomicity in code-signing chain
content: The entire pipeline is collapsed into one bash script because macOS code signing requires strict temporal ordering: nested XPC services must be signed before their parent .app, and the .app before DMG creation, with no intermediate state that could be cached or partially invalidated. A Makefile or build system with separate targets would risk stale signatures if a developer ran targets out of order, but this choice sacrifices incremental builds and makes the script harder to unit test.

title: Five-strategy fallback chain exists because no single brightness control API works across all Apple display hardware generations and third-party monitors
content: The subsystem probes DisplayServices (private Apple framework) first, then falls through DDC/CI, hybrid DDC+gamma, pure gamma, and finally software overlay. This ordering reveals that Apple has never provided a stable public API for display brightness, and DDC/CI support is inconsistent across monitors—particularly laptop internal displays and newer Apple Silicon external monitor implementations. The gamma fallback exists specifically because DDC/CI commands are silently ignored by many displays that report 'success,' requiring a side-effect verification through actual brightness readback.

title: Dynamically loads IOKit I2C symbols to survive OS updates that rename or remove private APIs
content: The subsystem uses dlopen/dlsym resolution at runtime rather than static linking against IOAVServiceWriteI2C and related symbols. This is a defensive maneuver against Apple's undocumented API churn—if symbols are renamed or removed in a macOS update, the module degrades gracefully (returns false) rather than failing to launch. Static linking would create a hard dependency that could break the entire application on OS upgrade. The tradeoff is complete loss of functionality if symbols disappear, with no fallback path.

title: Native Swift menu-bar form factor avoids sandboxing entitlements that would block HID and DDC access
content: A menu bar app is the documented delivery mechanism rather than a more conventional preference pane or background daemon. This choice is load-bearing: macOS App Sandbox would prohibit the HID device access and DDC-CI I2C writes that constitute core functionality, and a System Preferences pane would require code signing with the 'com.apple.security.device.usb' entitlement that is increasingly restricted to notarized developers with hardware partner relationships. The menu bar format lets the app operate as a regular user process with explicit TCC prompts, avoiding the sandbox while still presenting a native-feeling integration point.

title: Sparkle's sign_update requirement forces DMG recreation after notarization, creating an irreversible artifact chain
content: The documented flow requires producing an unsigned DMG, then codesigning, then recreating the DMG for notarization—because Sparkle's EdDSA signature must be computed over the final distributed artifact, but stapler modifies the DMG in-place after notarization. This creates a fragile manual checkpoint where the maintainer must track which DMG has which signature, explaining why the guide warns about 'manual DMG recreation' as a common failure point.

title: AppDelegate as centralized hardware event router creates single-point coupling to preserve mode-switching atomicity
content: All hardware events funnel through AppDelegate before dispatch to mode-specific controllers, rather than allowing transports to directly message controllers. This centralization ensures that mode transitions are atomic and mutually exclusive—critical for a physical knob where simultaneous volume and MIDI output would create ambiguous device state. The coupling cost is accepted because distributed routing would require distributed locking or state reconciliation for a shared hardware resource.

title: NSWorkspace live discovery in settings UI couples profile creation to the user's actual installed apps rather than a static allow-list
content: CustomModeSettingsView queries NSWorkspace for running/installed applications at profile creation time rather than shipping a predefined bundle ID list. This avoids maintenance burden for new apps but creates a dependency on the user's current system state, meaning profile setup is non-deterministic and may surface sandboxed or translocated apps differently across machines.

title: Normalized CC value tracking exists primarily to close the LED feedback loop, not for MIDI semantics
content: The data flow explicitly shows CC state feeding back to LED synchronization. This implies the module maintains shadow state of last-sent CC values not because MIDI requires it (MIDI is stateless fire-and-forget), but because the PowerMate's LED ring needs to reflect the current 'virtual knob' position. This creates a coupling where MIDIController must be queryable for current state, complicating what could otherwise be a pure translation layer.

title: Automatic reconnection logic is delegated to CBCentralManager rather than app-level state to exploit iOS's built-in bonding queue
content: The module implements reconnection at the CoreBluetooth layer instead of building a higher-level retry orchestrator. This trades control granularity for system integration: iOS handles background reconnection, power management, and coexists with other BLE apps without custom wake locks. The 'unimplemented' bonding persistence note suggests this was a deliberate scope cut—full bonding state would require keychain or NSUserDefaults complexity that conflicts with the goal of letting the OS own the radio.

title: Manual .app bundle assembly instead of `swift package generate-xcodeproj` preserves Sparkle rpath control
content: The script manually constructs the .app bundle and injects Sparkle rather than using Swift Package Manager's built-in Xcode project generation, because SPM does not expose sufficient control over `@rpath` entries and framework embedding locations required for notarization. This reveals that the project predates or bypasses SPM's 5.3+ binary target support, accepting the fragility of hardcoded paths in exchange for deterministic rpath fixup that Apple's notary service accepts.

title: Per-display gamma table capture/restore prevents color profile corruption when gamma-based dimming is released
content: The subsystem maintains separate gamma state per display identifier rather than applying a global gamma ramp because macOS display calibration profiles (including Night Shift and True Tone) are stored per-display in the window server. Restoring incorrect gamma tables would permanently distort color until reboot or recalibration. This design implies the author encountered gamma state leakage bugs where releasing one display's dimming affected others, likely on multi-monitor setups with mixed internal/external displays.

title: Explicitly excludes built-in displays to avoid conflicting with DisplayServices' exclusive brightness control
content: The subsystem filters out built-in displays rather than attempting universal brightness control because Apple's DisplayServices framework holds exclusive access to internal panel brightness on Apple Silicon, using a separate (undocumented) communication path. Attempting DDC/CI on built-in displays would fail silently or potentially interfere with system-managed dimming, Night Shift, and HDR tone mapping. The exclusion is a territorial concession to Apple's display stack, accepting a bifurcated architecture where external and internal displays follow entirely different control paths.

title: Global dispatch queue for HID input with main-queue forwarding reflects a deliberate latency-throughput tradeoff to avoid blocking IOKit's dedicated thread
content: The data flow specifies C callback on global queue then `DispatchQueue.main.async` for event delivery, rather than direct main-thread callback registration. This indicates awareness that IOKet input callbacks run on a constrained thread and must not block; the double-hop architecture sacrifices ~1-2ms latency to prevent audio/UI stutter from synchronous PowerMateManager processing.

title: Four-mode architecture masks HID-to-system-control impedance mismatch with per-app profiles
content: The Volume/Brightness/MIDI/Custom taxonomy collapses fundamentally different macOS integration surfaces—CoreAudio, DDC-CI, CoreMIDI, and Accessibility-API event injection—into a single rotary encoder abstraction. Per-application profiles are documented as a user-facing feature, but their real architectural function is to paper over the fact that no single mode works acceptably across all applications: DDC-CI monitors vary in command sets, Accessibility permissions are per-app and fragile, and MIDI mapping requires host software. The profile system lets users manually route around these integration failures rather than solving them generically.

title: Mouse-cursor positioning prioritizes discoverability over fixed-screen placement because PowerMate is a physical rotary device without on-screen focus
content: Unlike keyboard media keys that users associate with screen-center feedback, a USB rotary knob lacks inherent spatial anchoring in the user's mental model. Positioning the HUD under the cursor exploits the user's existing visual attention locus, compensating for the device's detachment from the display. This differs from Apple's fixed-center system HUD which assumes users are already looking at the menu bar or screen center after keypress.

title: Single-file engine consolidates profile dispatch to avoid cross-module synchronization of hardware state
content: The entire profile engine lives in one file (CustomModeEngine.swift) despite handling four distinct output protocols (MIDI, OSC, keyboard, volume). This suggests the PowerMate's physical state—rotation accumulation, press-and-hold timing, CC value smoothing—must remain coherent across output switches, and splitting across files would risk desynchronized state during rapid profile transitions when the frontmost app changes.

title: Manual release pipeline preserves single-maintainer operational control over Apple Developer ID credentials
content: The hand-operated notarization and appcast.xml steps prevent CI/CD secrets from holding a Developer ID private key, which would require either Apple ID 2FA automation (unreliable) or storing credentials in GitHub Actions (unacceptable for a solo maintainer's personal Apple account). The module explicitly documents 'manual' steps where automation would normally exist, suggesting the maintainer treats the Apple Developer account as a personal liability boundary rather than project infrastructure.

title: OSDOverlay feedback is decoupled from volume success to mask strategy failures and maintain hardware responsiveness
content: The data flow shows OSDOverlay receives display level independently of whether CoreAudio or AppleScript actually succeeded, implying the UI layer is deliberately optimistic. This hides per-strategy latency variance from users during rapid knob events, at the cost of potential visual-audio desync when AppleScript fallback fails silently. The design sacrifices consistency for perceived responsiveness on a physical control device where tactile feedback dominates.

title: Retained but unexposed settings window controller suggests planned UI expansion abandoned or deferred
content: The module retains a custom settings window controller that is never presented in the current UI, indicating either a partially-implemented feature or a deliberate decision to suppress advanced configuration. This is not dead code from oversight—the controller is actively instantiated and retained, suggesting the team anticipated user demand for granular settings but deprioritized the UI surface, likely to ship a minimal viable product. The hidden controller preserves the option to expose it with minimal code change.

title: GitHub Pages hosting trades update availability for zero infrastructure cost, accepting the risk that Pages outages or repo visibility changes break the auto-update channel
content: The module explicitly uses GitHub Pages as the serving layer with no CDN or fallback mentioned. This is a deliberate cost/risk tradeoff: Sparkle requires a static XML endpoint, and Pages provides HTTPS+global edge for free. The 'partial' status and manual steps suggest this is a small-team/project where operational simplicity outweighs reliability guarantees—if Pages fails, updates simply don't arrive, which is acceptable for a non-critical utility app.

title: Custom vector renderer avoids NSImage asset bundles to enable single-file Swift source distribution
content: The 24x24→18x18 scaling with Core Graphics path construction in a single .swift file suggests the icon system was designed to eliminate .xcassets or bundled PDF/SVG dependencies. This enables the entire PowerMateReborn utility to be distributed as a standalone source file or minimal binary without resource bundle packaging, which matters for a small hardware-utility app where installation friction directly impacts adoption.

title: Sparkle pinned to 2.5.0 avoids EdDSA key migration complexity
content: Sparkle 2.5.0 is the last version before the 2.6.x series introduced mandatory EdDSA signature requirements that would invalidate existing DSA-based update feeds. Pinning here defers a key rotation ceremony that would break auto-update for existing users unless the feed URL simultaneously serves dual-signed updates. The .process("Resources") bundling suggests Sparkle's XPC helpers and localizations are vendored directly rather than fetched at runtime, making version bumps a manual release-step decision.

title: Virtual source endpoint avoids requiring users to configure loopback MIDI drivers, reducing support burden
content: CoreMIDI virtual sources appear automatically to DAWs without IAC driver setup or third-party loopback software. This design trades the complexity of managing virtual endpoint lifecycle (client creation, source creation, cleanup on quit) against eliminating a common failure mode where users misconfigure MIDI routing. The 'partial' status likely reflects incomplete resource cleanup or endpoint persistence issues.

title: LED write completion is left unimplemented because the hardware's visual latency masks async acknowledgment needs
content: The module forwards LED commands fire-and-forget without waiting for peripheral confirmation. For a rotary knob with human-scale LED feedback, the 50-200ms human perception threshold dwarfs BLE write latency; adding completion handlers would complicate the state machine for no user-visible gain. The TODO comment about unimplemented completion handling marks this as a known acceptable debt rather than oversight.

title: Unsafe pointer bridging to C IOKit callbacks forces manual memory management because Swift's closure-based HID APIs were unavailable or broken in target macOS versions
content: The module uses raw `IOHIDManagerRegisterInputReportCallback` with an `Unmanaged<PowerMateUSBTransport>` passthrough rather than the modern `IOHIDDeviceInputReportWithTimeStampCallback` or queue-based APIs. This suggests the codebase targets macOS versions where Swift closure bridging to C function pointers was unreliable, forcing the `fromOpaque`/`toOpaque` dance that introduces the documented memory safety issues.

title: Network.framework UDP with connection caching avoids TCP head-of-line blocking for real-time audio sync
content: The module uses Network.framework's UDP rather than POSIX sockets or TCP-based OSC, caching NWConnection instances by host:port. This trades connection setup latency against the risk of packet loss, which is acceptable because OSC is designed as an unreliable, time-sensitive protocol where stale data is worse than missing data. The caching specifically targets the 'custom mode engine' and 'application delegate' as callers that likely emit rapid-fire transport commands (play/stop/scrub) where per-message DNS resolution or connection handshake would cause audible jitter.

title: Timer-based gesture detection on main runloop trades accuracy for UI thread affinity to avoid cross-thread delegate callback complexity
content: The gesture state machine uses Foundation.Timer on the main runloop rather than a dedicated queue or dispatch source timer, which creates the documented risk of missed gestures under UI load. This shape suggests the subsystem prioritizes guaranteed delegate callback execution on the main thread—required by AppDelegate, BrightnessController, and VolumeController—over temporal precision. A dedicated timer queue with main-thread dispatch would add re-entrancy risk and complicate the unprotected shared state access that already exists.

title: Documentation precedes implementation to attract hardware owners before Bluetooth stack is validated
content: The README claims full Bluetooth support and notarized releases despite the 'partial' component status and explicit gaps in Bluetooth validation. This suggests documentation serves as a recruitment funnel for Griffin PowerMate hardware owners on modern macOS, where the installed base of legacy USB devices is shrinking and Bluetooth-capable units command premium resale prices. The Sparkle appcast infrastructure is documented before it can deliver signed updates, indicating a 'build the landing page first' strategy common to hardware-resurrection projects that need community validation of device variants they cannot personally source.

title: Codable persistence for profiles implies user-editable configuration without a dedicated editor UI
content: The domain tag 'codable-persistence' and the data flow through CodableAppProfile suggest profiles are stored as serialized data rather than compiled code. This likely exists to let users share or hand-edit profiles as JSON/plist without the project maintaining a visual profile editor—trading rich UI for ecosystem extensibility and reduced maintenance burden.

title: Template image with automatic dark mode trades color expressiveness for App Store sandbox compliance
content: Using NSImage template rendering rather than explicit light/dark mode color variants avoids the need for private API or entitlements to detect menu bar appearance changes. The 'automatic dark mode' behavior is inherited from macOS's template image system, which sidesteps the need for appearance observation that could trigger App Store review scrutiny for a utility app with minimal UI surface area.

title: Monolithic framework linkage preserves runtime discoverability over binary size
content: Linking all nine frameworks explicitly in Package.swift rather than relying on transitive dependencies or weak linking ensures that `otool -L` on the built binary reveals the complete dependency surface for notarization and app store review. This trades ~2-3MB of binary bloat for auditability, since Apple reviewers flag binaries with dynamically loaded frameworks that don't appear in the load commands. The hardcoded macOS 13 minimum likely mirrors this conservative stance—avoiding `@available` runtime checks in favor of compile-time guarantees.

title: Hardcoded macOS 13.0 minimum avoids dynamic version resolution to prevent stale template syndrome
content: The template bakes in '13.0' rather than consuming the deployment target from build configuration, creating a deliberate friction point that forces manual review when dropping older macOS support. This prevents silent expansion of the supported version matrix that would complicate testing and increase support burden for a niche hardware accessory utility.

title: LED control via 1-byte output reports instead of feature reports implies Griffin's firmware lacks writable feature report descriptors, constraining atomic state updates
content: The module sends LED commands as output reports rather than using `IOHIDDeviceSetReport` with `kIOHIDReportTypeFeature`. This design constraint likely stems from the PowerMate's HID descriptor exposing LED brightness as an output endpoint only, preventing read-modify-write atomicity and forcing the subsystem to maintain last-known LED state in Swift rather than querying hardware.

title: Big-endian padded packet construction preserves compatibility with legacy OSC implementations that strictly enforce 4-byte alignment
content: The explicit big-endian byte ordering and 32-bit padding of OSC strings/blobs is retained despite Swift's native little-endian architecture and modern OSC libraries relaxing alignment rules. This conservatism suggests the module targets endpoints like Max/MSP, Pure Data, or older SuperCollider versions that crash or silently drop malformed packets rather than tolerating spec deviations. The padding cost (up to 3 bytes per string) is negligible for the small control payloads but prevents hard-to-debug interoperability failures across diverse audio software.

title: Single-file implementation in PowerMateManager.swift preserves gesture-LED atomicity by colocating state machine and broadcast logic, accepting the coupling cost
content: Despite spanning gesture recognition, multi-transport coordination, and LED feedback, the entire subsystem lives in one file with zero internal dependencies. This rejects decomposition into separate gesture/LED modules, likely because LED brightness commands must be broadcast atomically with gesture completion to prevent visual desync across USB and BLE transports. Splitting would expose the unprotected shared state to cross-module synchronization, which the current design avoids by keeping all mutation in one compilation unit.

title: Reusable geometric primitives (knobs, rays, wave arcs) encode hardware product semantics without trademarked imagery
content: The abstract shape vocabulary—knobs, rays, wave arcs, dot markers—appears designed to evoke the physical Griffin PowerMate device's rotary dial and LED feedback patterns without reproducing Griffin's actual product iconography or logo. This provides recognizable hardware affordance cues while avoiding trademark infringement, which is critical for an unofficial 'Reborn' successor project operating without original manufacturer endorsement.

title: GitHub Pages hosting reference in template diverges from production to enable fork-based beta distribution
content: The template points to GitHub Pages while production uses raw URLs, suggesting the template serves dual purpose as both production stencil and community fork enabler. This lets third-party builders or beta channels host independent appcasts without modifying Sparkle's feed URL at build time, reducing friction for unofficial builds that still want auto-update.

title: Unsafe pointer bridging to C IOKit callbacks forces manual retain cycle management
content: PowerMateUSBTransport.swift registers IOKit HID input report callbacks via IOHIDManagerRegisterInputReportCallback with an Unmanaged<PowerMateUSBTransport> passthrough to the raw C callback. This avoids the modern IOHIDDeviceInputReportWithTimeStampCallback or queue-based API that would permit automatic closure bridging, because the transport layer predates or deliberately excludes Swift's block-based IOKit wrappers. The consequence is manual retain/release balancing: the callback context must be explicitly retained on registration and released on deinit to prevent dangling pointers or leaks.

title: Custom NSWindow HUD replication accepts visual fidelity loss to avoid private OSDUIHelper entitlements
content: The on-screen display is a from-scratch NSWindow implementation using public AppKit APIs (translucency, SF Symbols, segmented level bar) rather than Apple's private OSDUIHelper/BezelServices framework. This is an app store distribution constraint: the private entitlements required for system OSD are unavailable to sandboxed or notarized apps. The constraint is load-bearing because it forces acceptance of visual mismatch with native macOS OSD and requires deliberate decoupling of display feedback from actual hardware success—VolumeController shows optimistic UI even when CoreAudio or AppleScript strategies fail, because the overlay cannot access system-level success signals.
